stem: A53-year-old woman who has rheumatoid arthritis is referred to the Respiratory Clinic with progressive shortness of breath, cough and sputum production. Auscultation of the chest reveals coarse crackles and wheeze, more marked on the left-hand side. Investigation Result Normal values Chest X-ray Bronchial wall thickening High-resolution CT Centrilobular nodules, bronchial wall thickening, expiratory air trapping, more marked on the left Forced expiratory volume in one second(FEV) 280 litres/min, no improvement with salbutamol 490 litres/min predicted What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Obliterative bronchiolitis is seen in patients with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis and is associated with centrilobular inflammatory nodule formation, bronchial wall thickening and expiratory air trapping. It fits here with a significantly reduced FEVwhich is not reversed with salbutamol and one side of the chest is often more severely affected than the other. Optimal therapy has not been determined, with macrolide antibiotics, glucocorticoids and cytotoxics all having been trialled, with little evidence to support their use. Rheumatoid arthritis Media explanations.

stem: A 35-year-old man who has long-standing psoriasis presents to the Emergency Department with erythroderma. His temperature is 38.4℃ and BP 100/70 mmHg. His heart rate is 100 bpm and regular. He has generalised erythema with fine skin scaling compared to his usual psoriasis. He is given IV fluids, corticosteroids and analgesia. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 142 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 11.2×10/ 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 189×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 115μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L What is the most appropriate disease-modifying intervention for this patient?
explanation: Ciclosporin is recommended as the initial disease-modifying therapy in erythrodermic psoriasis, the diagnosis here. Erythroderma can be precipitated by the withdrawal of corticosteroids, the use of lithium, antimalarials and some viral infections. It may be associated with a Th2-predominant phenotype,accounting for the utility of agents such as ciclosporin. Infliximab is a potential alternative where ciclosporin is contraindicated or ineffective. Erythroderma explanations.

stem: A 73-year-old man is readmitted to the Emergency Department four days after discharge following an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). He was on the Medical Ward for five days before discharge. His temperature is 37.9℃, BP 148/84 mmHg and heart rate 94 bpm. His chest is hyperexpanded, with quiet wheeze on auscultation. His respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 152 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 9.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 132 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 45 mg/l 10 mg/l What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: Viral exacerbation of COPD auscultation of the chest, a viral exacerbation of COPD is the most likely cause of his symptoms. Unfortunately, he is likely to have been exposed to the virus during his hospital stay and developed symptoms shortly after discharge. Management is the same as for any other COPD exacerbation, with use of bronchodilators and corticosteroids. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Media explanations.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of diarrhoea with blood and mucus. He is opening his bowels 10 or more times per day. He returned from a holiday to India two weeks earlier. His BP is 90/50 mmHg and his heart rate is 98 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft, although there is marked lower abdominal tenderness. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 150 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 13.1×109/L 4-11×109/L Platelets(PLT) 295×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 122μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Amoebic dysentery fits with the abdominal pain, diarrhoea with blood and mucus and raised WCC seen here. The disease is endemic in India and is spread via the faeco-oral route. Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites invade large bowel mucosa and lead to the formation of flask-shaped ulcers. These are responsible for the blood and mucus seen per rectum. Many patients are asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic and in a small number of cases, the infection progresses to form an amoebic liver abscess. Metronidazole and tinidazole are both potential interventions. Amoebiasis explanations.

stem: 1Y:29 o.L Y321 A 25-year-old woman who usually has mild asthma presents to the Respiratory Clinic with worsening shortness of breath, wheeze and a cough productive of mucus and blood over the past few weeks, as well as general malaise. Her temperature is 37.8°℃; her BP is 123/82 mmHg and her heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. There is wheeze, as well as inspiratory crackles, on auscultation of the chest. What is the most likely diagnosis? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 132 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.1×109/L 4-11×10/L Eosinophils 2.3×10/L 0.05-0.5×10/L Platelets (PLT) 209×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Chest X-ray Patchy pulmonary infiltrates
explanation: Aspergilosis explanations.

stem: A52-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with intensely itchy small red papules on the flexural surfaces of both wrists. They are shiny on the top,with white streaks. Examination of the inside of the mouth reveals a number of raised white lesions with a lace-like trabecular pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The itchy papules on flexural skin surfaces and lacy white lesions within the mouth are consistent with lichen planus. The exact cause of lichen planus remains to be identified, but it is thought to be a T cell- mediated autoimmune condition. Symptomatic treatment for itching with antihistamines may be required and topical steroids are the usual first-line anti-inflammatory intervention. Systemic agents, including ciclosporin and azathioprine, may be required for patients with resistant lesions. Q.

stem: A 19-year-old man attends the dentist for removal of a wisdom tooth. He had a significant bleed following a previous dental extraction and has been diagnosed with von Willebrand's disease. He does not usually have any issues with bleeding. What is the most appropriate prophylaxis before this patient's next tooth extraction?
explanation: Desmopressin temporarily increases factor VII and von Willebrand factor levels by releasing endothelial stores. It can be given intranasally or parenterally. It can be used to treat bleeding complications but is more commonly used as a prophylactic agent, eg before tooth extraction. Tranexamic acid is another option for prophylaxis. Desmopressin is ineffective in type 3 von Willebrand's disease, as there is no von Willebrand factor level to boost.

stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted to the Care of the Elderly Ward with left lower lobe pneumonia. He is very restless, fidgeting continuously and trying to get out of the bed. According to his daughter, he has had a poor appetite recently. He appears to have been faecally incontinent. His BMI is 29 kg/m. Which feature adds most to this patient's risk of pressure sores?
explanation: Incontinence is a major risk factor for pressure sores. Complete continence or catheterisation attracts a score of O and urinary incontinence alone a score of 1.Faecal incontinence attracts a score of 2 and both urinary and faecal incontinence a score of 3. Q.

stem: A 23-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with medullary thyroid carcinoma.This was picked up on family screening after her 28-year-old sister was diagnosed with the condition.
explanation: Activating point mutations in RET can lead to the development of both familial medullary thyroid carcinoma and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2(both types 2A and 2B).The position of the point mutations correlates closely with disease phenotype. RETplays an important role in the normal development of the kidneys and enteric nervous system. Chromosomal rearrangements which generate a fusion gene, which also activates RETkinase, are seen in non-small cell lung cancer. Q.

stem: A 67-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with central crushing chest pain and inferior ST-segment elevation on his ECG. Around 15 minutes into his admission, he develops complete heart block. Which coronary artery is most likely to have been occluded?
explanation: Inferior myocardial infarction is caused by right coronary artery occlusion in 80% of cases. The right coronary artery is also responsible for blood supply to the AV node and occlusion can therefore result in complete heart block. Around 18% of inferior myocardial infarctions result from left circumflex artery occlusion. Wrap- around infarctions involving the inferior territory are also seen from the left anterior descending coronary artery. Q.

stem: A 23-year-old Egyptian man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with oral and genital ulceration and a recent episode of uveitis. Examination reveals erythema nodosum on both shins. He suffered a left lower limb DVT some 12 months ago. What human leukocyte antigen(HLA) type is most likely to be found in this patient?
explanation: This patient has oral and genital ulceration, uveitis, erythema nodosum and thrombophilia. This fits with a diagnosis of Behcet's disease, which is associated with an increased prevalence of the HLA-B51 subtype. Testing for B51 is, however, not specific enough to confirm a diagnosis of Behcet's disease, which is made clinically. Around 25% of patients with Behcet's disease are antiphospholipid antibody positive and active disease is associated with elevated inflammatory markers. Corticosteroids are effective for acute disease flares, although over the longer term, steroid-sparing medications, such as azathioprine, should be introduced. Q.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department for review.He says he felt something pop in his chest the previous evening and is concerned that he may have a problem. He has no pain and no shortness of breath. Auscultation of the chest is unremarkable. A chestX-ray reveals a 1-cm rim of air on the left-hand side. Oxygen saturation is 98% measured by pulse oximetry. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Air aspiration, then admit for overnight oxygen
explanation: This patient has a small primary pneumothorax which is asymptomatic. Given it is only 1 cm, it is safe to consider discharge and review in the Outpatient Department in 2-4 weeks. Only larger or symptomatic lesions require air aspiration. Q.

stem: A32-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with confusion, neck stiffness and severe headache. Her husband says she seems increasingly confused and agitated, particularly over the last 48 hours. Her temperature is 38.1°℃;her BP is 122/82 mmHg and her heart rate is 88 bpm and regular. She has obvious neck stiffness and photophobia.A magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) scan of the brain suggests bilateral inflammation affecting the inferomedial temporal lobes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Herpes simplex encephalitis is consistent with the clinical picture seen here, with pyrexia, headache and progressive confusion. Inferomedial temporal lobe changes, with signs of oedema and inflammation on MRI scan, are typical of the condition. It is important to recognise the disease as early as possible because neurological deficit is related to a delay in initiating intravenous aciclovir therapy. A dose of aciclovir of 10 mg/kg every eight hours is appropriate. Q.

stem: A 22-year-old man is reviewed in the Gastroenterology Clinic following a colonoscopy for diarrhoea with blood and mucus. He has been opening his bowels 4-6 times per day for the last six months. The colonoscopy confirms the presence of proctitis only and a biopsy showed inflammation, with evidence of cryptitis and crypt abscess. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation: The likely diagnosis is ulcerative colitis. Rectal mesalamine is the initial treatment of choice for mild to moderate symptoms where there is proctitis only. As an enema, the recommended dosage is 4 g every night for 3-6 weeks; as a suppository, the recommended dose is 1 g. Where symptoms are not controlled, then rectal prednisolone can be considered. Given the disease is locally confined at this stage, systemic therapy with attendant side-effects can be potentially avoided. Q.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of persistent dull headaches which are worse first thing in the morning and last thing at night. They are relieved by getting up and moving about and made worse by straining on the toilet. She has transient greying out of her vision on stooping or bending down and intermittent diplopia. Her BP is 155/90 mmHg. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilloedema. Her BMI is 35 kg/m. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: In an obese young woman, severe postural headache with papilloedema and greying out of vision should suggest idiopathic intracranial hypertension until proven otherwise. CT reveals normal or reduced ventricular size. Lumbar puncture reveals raised intracranial pressure of25 cm,with normal constituents. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis should be ruled out with a CT or magnetic resonance venogram. Q.

stem: A 29-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department having vomited up an egg cup-full of fresh blood. He says this occurred after the fourth episode of vomiting when there was extreme retching, but little material expelled. He tells you that he ate a kebab that had been left out overnight and wonders if this is the cause of his vomiting. His BP is 135/72 mmHg and his heart rate is 70 bpm and regular. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Mallory-Weiss tears are longitudinal lacerations which occur in the distal oesophagus and proximal stomach as a result of persistent and severe retching. They result in vomiting of small volumes of fresh blood, consistent with the clinical picture seen here. The stable picture, with respect to pulse and blood pressure,is also consistent with relatively minor bleeding. In the majority of cases, no treatment is required. Q.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has had chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain and weight loss over the last six months. Investigations have revealed iron deficiency anaemia and borderline low calcium levels. ILeal biopsy reveals non-caseating granuloma formation and pyloric gland metaplasia. The distal colon and rectum appear to be clear of inflammation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The chronic abdominal pain, diarrhoea and weight loss seen here are typical symptoms associated with Crohn's disease. Characteristic changes of Crohn's disease include non-caseating granuloma formation and the pyloric gland metaplasia seen here. Glucocorticoids are recommended to induce remission after a first presentation with Crohn's disease and azathioprine is the usual first-line steroid-sparing agent to be introduced. Q.

stem: A 47-year-old man with cirrhosis has become acutely unwell 10 minutes into a platelet transfusion. He has a temperature of 38.6℃.His BP is 80/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 110 bpm and regular. There are bilateral inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: Platelets are stored at temperatures between 22℃ and 24℃, which significantly increases the risk of bacterial contamination, compared to packed red cells which are stored at temperatures between 2℃ and 6 ℃. According to a study from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from the United States, up to one in 2000-2500 platelet units may be contaminated with bacteria. Bacterial contamination fits with the severe symptoms seen here, with marked pyrexia,hypotension, tachycardia and pulmonary oedema. The platelet transfusion should be stopped, the bag sent for microscopy and culture and the patient treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Dificulty:Average.

stem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the Respiratory Clinic complaining of shortness of breath, a cough and wheeze. She says symptoms are worse when she attends her job as an animal technician and are better when she is off work. Examination in the clinic is unremarkable. Her peak flow is 520 L/min (535 L/min predicted). What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Twice-daily peak flow monitoring and review
explanation: This patient's symptoms suggest she may have occupational asthma, potentially due to exposure to animal allergens.Improvement in her symptoms when she is off work is characteristic of occupational disease. Initiating treatment without confirming the diagnosis is not advised because if there is continued exposure to an allergen, then intervention will be unsuccessful. Once occupational asthma is confirmed by significantly worsened peak flows during the working week, then her working environment should be examined with respect to measures to minimise allergen exposure. If this is not completely possible, then a transfer to another role within the organisation should be considered. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A 69-year-old man is reviewed on the Admissions Ward the morning after admission with urinary retention. His General Practitioner had already identified a smoothly enlarged prostate and his prostate-specific antigen is 3.0(4.5μg/L). A decision is made to start him on finasteride. What is the most likely adverse effect of finasteride therapy?
explanation: Gynaecomastia is a well-recognised side-effect of finasteride therapy. It is seen in 0.5% of patients who take it in the first year and in 1.8% of patients in years two, three and four of therapy. Finasteride is a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor which reduces production of dihydrotestosterone, thereby decreasing androgen levels. Other side-effects include erectile dysfunction and decreased libido. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A32-year-old woman with long-standing type I diabetes comes to the Emergency Department complaining of blurred vision affecting her left eye. She smokes 20 cigarettes per day. Her BP is 145/90 mmHg. Her latest glycated haemoglobin is 62 mmol/mol(48 mmol/mol). Retinal photography reveals neovascularisation and hard exudates close to the macula. What is the most important next step?
explanation: This patient has neovascularisation close to the macula and is at imminent risk of sight-threatening retinal haemorrhage. For this reason, focal photocoagulation is the most appropriate next step.This can be followed later with more widespread laser therapy to further reduce the risk of new vessel formation over 2-3 sessions. Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy may be of value for macular oedema but is less effective in this situation, compared to photocoagulation. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A 28-year-old Nursing Assistant attends Occupational Health for advice because she has served food on five occasions during a weekend to a man who was later found to have active pulmonary tuberculosis(TB). She has had a bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination some years ago. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassurance and advice about symptoms of TB
explanation: The Nursing Assistant is described as a casual contact for the purposes of TB infection risk. Guidance suggests she needs only be given advice about symptoms of TB infection, as the risks of her developing the disease is very low. A close contact where the risk is much higher is defined as staff who have undertaken any of the following procedures: Dificuty.

stem: A 64-year-old woman who has type ll diabetes has been prescribed 1 litre of 5% dextrose over six hours as fluid replacement. What is the glucose content of 1 litre of 5% dextrose?
explanation: Dextrose 5% contains 50 mg of glucose per millilitre of solution, which translates to a total glucose content of 50 mg in 1 litre of fluid. This is adequate to meet the carbohydrate needs in a patient with diabetes.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the Oncology Clinic for review,following surgery for invasive breast cancer. What is the most useful biomarker to monitor for metastatic disease?
explanation: CA 15-3 represents a series of mucins which are overexpressed in glandular cancers, particularly breast cancer. It can be used to monitor patients at high risk of metastatic disease or to measure overall burden of disease in patients who already have metastases, particularly bony lesions. A rise in CA 15-3 level may occur a few months before bony lesions can be identified on radiological imaging. The upper end of the normal range for CA 15-3 is 30 units/ml. Q. Answered Flagged o.

stem: A72-year-old man, who is awaiting a percutaneous gastrostomy for feeding because of a bulbar palsy, is admitted to the Gastroenterology Ward. He is nil by mouth. He weighs 65 kg. Which of the following approximates best to this patient's daily potassium requirements?
explanation: In a patient with normal potassium levels who is not suffering from excessive losses, potassium replacement requirements are approximately 1 mmol/kg/day. In a 65-kg man, this is 65 mmol and 64 mmol is the closest answer to this.Where there are gastrointestinal losses, a higher level of potassium replacement is needed.

stem: A 42-year-old amateur rugby player presents to the Emergency Department with an acutely swollen and painful left knee. He is unable to weight-bear or flex the knee beyond 30 degrees. He has a temperature of 38.2℃.There is erythema over the knee and a large joint effusion. Aspiration reveals 1700 cells/μl,85% of which are neutrophils. Gram staining is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has a significant elevation in synovial fluid cell count and marked symptoms of monoarthritis.

stem: A 49-year-old woman attends the Oncology Clinic to discuss further management of her breast cancer following a lumpectomy. She has read about trastuzumab. Which receptor found on biopsy determines the response to trastuzumab?
explanation: The HER2 receptoris a member of the human epidermal growth factor receptor family. Signalling through the receptor promotes cellular proliferation and downregulates cell apoptosis. Trastuzumab binds with high specificity and affinity to subdomain IV-this is the juxtamembrane region of the extracellular domain of HER2.Binding of trastuzumab to HER2 inhibits HER2 signalling, which is dependent on ligand binding and prevents proteolytic cleavage of its extracellular domain, an activation mechanism of HER2.This, in turn, serves to downregulate cellular proliferation and increase apoptosis of cancer cells.

stem: A 49-year-old woman who was brought to the Emergency Department earlier with dull central chest ache following a road traffic accident, in which the air bag went off and injured her chest, deteriorates. She is newly hypotensive, with a blood pressure of 90/50 mmHg and her heart rate is 110 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are muffled and her jugular venous pressure (JVP) is elevated. An echocardiogram performed three hours earlier was reported as unremarkable. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient has developed a traumatic pericardial effusion as a result of the road traffic accident. In the absence of a wound, ventricular aneurysm or aortic dissection,it is appropriate to consider pericardiocentesis as an initial intervention. This will remove blood and pericardial fluid from the sac and reduce pressure on the left ventricle, allowing it to function more efficiently.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is reviewed in the Endocrinology Clinic. She is thought to suffer from a syndrome of partial thyroid hormone resistance. What is the location of the thyroid hormone receptor?
explanation: The thyroid hormone receptor is a nuclear receptor which is activated by the binding of thyroid hormone. The thyroid hormone receptor affects the regulation of gene transcription and translation. It consists of four domains: DNA binding, hinge, ligand binding and transactivation. The transactivation domain allows the receptor to bind other transcription factors, apart from thyroid hormone.

stem: A74-year-old man, who has metastatic cancer and acute-on-chronic renal impairment, is admitted with decreased consciousness. He is currently taking slow-release morphine twice a day. Which morphine metabolite accumulates in renal impairment leading to respiratory depression?
explanation: Morphine is metabolised by the liver into morphine-3-glucuronide,morphine-6-glucuronide and normorphine. ALl three metabolites can accumulate in renal impairment. Morphine-3-glucuronide makes up 55% of the metabolites, morphine-6-glucuronide 10% and normorphine 4%.Around 10% of the parent compound is left unchanged. Morphine-3-glucuronide has low affinity for opiate receptors and may actually stimulate respiration and normorphine has very little opiate activity. Morphine-6-glucuronide is recognised to be a respiratory depressant and effects in reducing the respiratory rate are thought to be more marked in renal impairment.

stem: A72-year-old woman is reviewed on the General Medical Ward after a spell on the Intensive Therapy Unit (ITU) with Gram-negative sepsis. She was treated with gentamicin and is thought to have suffered gentamicin toxicity as her creatinine level has risen to 320μmol/L from a previously stable level of 150 μmol/L. Where are the cells affected by gentamicin toxicity located?
options: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
explanation: This is the main site of damage related to gentamicin toxicity. Gentamicin leads to necrosis of tubular cells predominantly in the proximal tubule because it is retained in cells along the S1 and S2 segments and is not cleared by glomerular filtration. Mild toxicity leads to accumulation of phospholipids in lysosomes and enlargement of cellular organelles. More severe toxicity leads to focal cellular necrosis of epithelial cells, followed by inflammation and fibrosis.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic because his eczema is not responding to therapy with topical corticosteroids or topical tacrolimus. He still has extensive erythema, with skin cracking and bleeding affecting the flexural surface of both arms and both hands. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Ciclosporin, azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil are all potential treatment options for resistant eczema. One or more agents are usually trialled before moving on to monoclonal options, such as tralokinumab, or to JAK inhibitors such as baricitinib. Doses of between 2 and 3 mg/kg/day of ciclosporin are initiated to treat eczema, with slow weaning once remission has been achieved. In patients who do not respond, switching to a monoclonal option could be considered. Concomitant medications should be reviewed because of the risk of CYP3A4 drug interactions.

stem: A 42-year-old woman who is in remission from leukaemia presents to the Rheumatology Clinic complaining of progressively worsening pain affecting her left groin and anterior thigh. She says it began gradually and has steadily built up over the last few months. The patient is unable to move her hip more than a few degrees due to pain. What is the most useful investigation?
options: MRI of the left hip and pelvis
explanation: This patient is in remission from leukaemia. As part of treatment, she is likely to have been exposed to high doses of corticosteroids. This puts her at increased risk of avascular necrosis of the hip which is associated with progressively worsening pain affecting the groin and anterior thigh.No laboratory tests are valuable in assessing avascular necrosis,but MRI is very sensitive in early disease, demonstrating decreased signal intensity in the subchondral region on T1-weighted scans and high signal intensity on T2-weighted scans, suggesting oedema. Iloprost,hyperbaric oxygen therapy and extracorporeal shock wave therapy may all be beneficial in early disease, although osteotomy and eventually hip replacement are required in many cases.

stem: Which retroperitoneal structure is directly in contact with the anterior surface of the left kidney?
explanation: The central portion of the anterior surface of the left kidney is directly in contact with the pancreas, which is a retroperitoneal structure.

stem: A39-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after being found unconscious following an overdose of antifreeze. She is treated with fomepizole. What is the mode of action of fomepizole?
options: Competitive inhibitor of the gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA)/benzodiazepine receptor complex
explanation: Fomepizole is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase. It has the advantage that it can be used in methanol and ethylene glycol overdoses without worsening intoxication. Ethylene glycol undergoes initial transformation by alcohol dehydrogenase to glycolaldehyde. It is then transformed by aldehyde dehydrogenase to glycolic acid, which is then further metabolised to oxalic acid. Oxalic acid causes severe acidosis and can lead to precipitation of calcium oxalate in the kidneys and other tissues.

stem: A 35-year-old woman who takes methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis attends the Emergency Department with her husband. He is extremely worried about her after a recent bout of influenza. She uses her foot to flush the toilet and washes her hands 8-10 times per day, suggesting to him that they are never clean. She wears a mask around the house because of fear of infection. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient's repetitive handwashing and beliefs around cleanliness which require her to use her foot to flush the toilet are consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder. Individualised CBT is the initial intervention of choice. In patients who do not respond to CBT alone,a SSRI could be considered. Clomipramine is an option in patients who fail to respond to SSRls.

stem: A 29-year-old woman, who has World Health Organization (WHO) type 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension, is commenced on ambrisentan for control of her symptoms. What is the mode of action of ambrisentan?
explanation: Ambrisentan is a selective endothelin A receptor antagonist, with 4000-fold greater selectivity for the endothelin A versus the endothelin B receptor. The endothelin A receptor mediates vasoconstriction and sodium retention when it binds to endothelin-1 and the endothelin B receptor mediates degradation of endothelin-1 and vasodilatation. Like other drugs in the endothelin antagonist class, ambrisentan is contraindicated in pregnancy-it is a first-trimester teratogen.

stem: A31-year-old car mechanic has been found unconscious in his garage and is brought to the Emergency Department. His BP is 90/50 mmHg and his heart rate is 110 bpm and regular. What is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 142 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 9.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 190×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 135μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Bicarbonate(HCO) 16 mmol/L 22-32 mmol/L Chloride (Cl-) 103 mmol/l 96-106 mmol/l
explanation: This patient's job as a mechanic means he is likely to have easy access to antifreeze (ethylene glycol). This leads to a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis. Here the anion gap is 4.9+143-16-103=28.9.A value of 12 is the threshold for defining a raised anion gap. Patients with ethylene glycol poisoning should be managed with fomepizole, an inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with facial oedema. He tells you he had a respiratory tract infection a few days earlier and this is the third episode he has had over the past three years. On the two previous occasions, his symptoms have responded to corticosteroids. His BP is 124/72 mmHg and his heart rate is 72 bpm and regular. What is the most likely diagnosis? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 142 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine dipstick Blood negative, protein 3+
explanation: Minimal change disease is associated with facial oedema and proteinuria and usually presents initially in childhood or teenage years. It is thought to be a T cell-mediated disorder which leads to damage to glomerular epithelial foot processes. In turn, there is decreased synthesis of polyanions and loss of the normal barrier which prevents loss of albumin into the urine. The majority of patients respond to high-dose corticosteroids within two weeks and remission of proteinuria is seen within up to 16 weeks in adults. Hypertension and resistant proteinuria should be treated with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a patch of skin on his lower chest that has fine skin scaling and mild erythema. It is around 8 cm in diameter. There is mild itching over the skin changes. He has an older patch on his back that has lost skin pigmentation. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: This patient's macular lesion with fine skin scaling and erythema on the chest, as well as the older depigmented lesion on his back, is suggestive of pityriasis versicolor, caused by the fungus Malassezia. Ketoconazole shampoo is applied to the affected area and left on for 3-5minutes before washing off; this is repeated daily for five days. Resistant cases could be treated with an oral antifungal agent such as itraconazole.

stem: A 62-year-old man is diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's disease following gradually progressive memory loss and mood change. His brother is 61 years old and has Alzheimer's disease. His father was diagnosed with the disease at the age of 59 years. What is the likely genetic basis for their Alzheimer's disease?
explanation: APOE e4 allele carriage is associated with an increased risk of late-onset Alzheimer's disease and may also be associated with a shift in time to an earlier presentation with the disease. Studies suggest that the risk of Alzheimer's disease is most increased for the 61- to 65-year age group. It is not known how the e4 allele confers excess risk, but it may increase the propensity for Alzheimer's plaques to form. A greater incremental risk of Alzheimer's disease is seen in patients who carry two e4 alleles, compared to those who carry one.

stem: A 49-year-old man has a cardiac arrest. He was admitted one hour earlier with symptoms and signs of a large pulmonary embolus, which has been confirmed on computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA). He has no pulse and is making no respiratory effort. An ECG reveals normal-shaped complexes, with a rate of around 140.1 mg of adrenaline is administered. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Alteplase 50 mg IV over one minute
Alteplase 100 mg IV over two hours
Normal saline 1 litre IV over 15 minutes
explanation: This dosing regimen is consistent with the PEAPETT study where a half-dose of alteplase was given as a bolus over one minute in patients who were in cardiorespiratory arrest. During a 34-month period,23 patients with pulseless electrical activity were treated in the study and at 22 months,87% of patients were still alive. No recurrent venous thromboembolism or bleeding was seen during hospitalisation or at follow- up. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation for 60-90 minutes after thrombolytic medication should be considered.

stem: An 18-year-old man is referred to the Genetics Clinic because of nosebleeds and recent haemoptysis. He tells you that his sister and father suffer from a similar condition and his father has actually had a number of GI haemorrhages. What is the most likely inheritance of this condition?
explanation: The bleeding pattern in the family affecting both the respiratory tract and the Gl tract and the fact that three first-degree relatives are affected raise the possibility of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia(HHT), which follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. It is associated with abnormal formation of blood vessels, including arteriovenous malformations and mutations in five or more genes have been identified that cause the clinical phenotype. Mutations in the ENG gene, which produces endoglin, result in HHT type 1.

stem: A 27-year-old man, who returned from a 3-week holiday to Ghana three days ago, is brought to the Emergency Department. He is drowsy and confused and has jaundiced sclerae. His temperature is 39.5°℃; his BP is 90/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 98 bpm and regular. There are bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest and his abdomen is generally tender. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 72 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 11.5×109/L 4-11×10/l Platelets(PLT) 75×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 164μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 2.9 mmol/l 4 mmol/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Malaria Media explanations In a patient who has been to Ghana for a considerable period and who presents with severe pyrexia, evidence of haemolysis, jaundice and renal failure,falciparum malaria should be excluded. Thick and thin films should be performed and rapid diagnostic tests are now also available. Hypoglycaemia is seen in severe malaria and is a prognostic indicator. Parasitaemia is also a key indicator of prognosis and patients with parasite levels above 2% should be treated aggressively with intravenous therapy. IV artesunate is the treatment of choice.

stem: An 82-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with a hypoglycaemic episode. She is currently taking gliclazide. What is the mode of action of gliclazide?
explanation: Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea which binds to adenosine triphosphate(ATP)-sensitive potassium channels on the surface of beta cells, causing them to close. This, in turn, drives the opening of voltage-gated calcium channels and an influx of calcium into beta cells. The influx of calcium leads to increased fusion of insulin granules with the cell membrane and glucose-independent insulin release. This can, of course, lead to an increased risk of hypoglycaemia, particularly in the elderly and patients with chronic renal impairment.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the clinic with blurred vision and intolerance of bright lights. Examination reveals a dilated right pupil, which does not react to light or accommodation. Eye movements are normal and there is no ptosis. He says he can see out of the right eye but finds bright lights difficult. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation: The dilated pupil that does not react to light or to accommodation is suggestive of a partial third nerve palsy. This raises the possibility of microvascular compromise or compression of the third cranial nerve and should prompt urgent referral for neuroimaging. While microvascular compromise is the most common painless cause, other possible painful causes include compression from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm or malignancy. Therefore, urgent non-invasive angiography is required.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic following three miscarriages in the past two years. She also suffered a DVT four years ago, for which she took warfarin for six months and suffers from joint pains, for which she takes naproxen. She says she does not like to go out in the sun because she tends to burn. Her fingers are slightly stiff and painful on palpation, but no other significant abnormalities are noted. What is the most likely cause of this patient's miscarriages? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 122 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count(WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 110×10/L 150-400×109/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 135 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Urine dipstick Blood 1+, protein 1+
explanation: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Media explanations This patient's sensitivity to the sun, coupled with recurrent miscarriages, joint pains and low PLT counts, is suggestive of possible systemic lupus erythematosus. The elevated Cr level, blood in the urine and proteinuria raise the possibility of lupus nephritis. Autoantibody testing,including antinuclear, anti-double- stranded DNA and antiphospholipid antibodies, is indicated. Possible options for treatment of lupus nephritis include mycophenolate and ciclosporin. If she plans further pregnancies, then both aspirin and low- molecular-weight heparin are indicated to reduce the risk of miscarriage.

stem: A76-year-old woman with chronic confusion on the Care of the Elderly Ward has fallen out of bed for the third time in the past two days. She is awaiting placement in a nursing home. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Placing the mattress on the floor
explanation: This patient is chronically confused, meaning that drug treatment is unlikely to have a major impact on her symptoms in the short term. The main risk is in falling from a height and this risk can be minimised by placing the mattress on the floor. Where possible, lighting should be optimised and the patient moved to the quietest area of the ward, with close nursing support.

stem: A45-year-old woman who has systemic sclerosis and suffers from Raynaud's phenomenon presents to the clinic complaining of worsening symptoms despite nifedipine therapy. She has peripheral calcinosis, early fibrotic changes affecting her lungs and reflux oesophagitis. What is the most appropriate additional intervention?
explanation: Phosphodiesterase type 5(PDE5) inhibitors, such as sildenafil, may be useful in treating patients with Raynaud's symptoms which are resistant to nifedipine therapy alone. It has been shown to be well tolerated and to have a significant impact on capillary blood flow and symptoms.

stem: A 59-year-old man returns to the Cardiology Clinic for review after starting metoprolol for chronic stable angina. Unfortunately, he has only had a small reduction in his resting heart rate and feels there has not been much impact on his symptoms.
explanation: ADRB1 is the gene for the beta-1 adrenoreceptor. One important function of the beta-1 receptor is to increase the heart rate via receptors found within the sinoatrial node. Two locations for polymorphisms in the ADRB1 gene have been shown to predict the heart rate response to beta-blockers in Caucasians. Both missense polymorphisms for both the'14 and'13 genes are associated with a reduced heart rate response to beta-blockade and may be associated with an increased susceptibility to vascular disease and type ll diabetes.

stem: A 20-year-old man is referred to the Endocrine Clinic for the management of his diabetes. He presented to his General Practitioner with a recurrent genital Candida infection and was found to have a fasting plasma glucose of 7.2 mmol/L(7.0 mmol/L). His BMI is 22 kg/m. Investigation Result Islet autoantibodies Negative Maturity-onset diabetes of the young(MODY) genetic testing HNF-1 alpha mutation-positive What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation: This patient has HNF-1 alpha MODY, the most common cause of the diseasein people of European ancestry, making up around 70% of cases.HNF-1 alpha is a transcription factor which controls the genes responsible for the development and differentiation of beta cells. Sulfonylureas can restore insulin secretory capacity in patients with HNF-1 alpha MODY for many years, staving off the need for insulin therapy, which,in turn, makes gliclazide the initial therapy of choice here.

stem: A 64-year-old man, who has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medications, is reviewed in the Medical Assessment Unit. He presented 24 hours earlier with acute-onset fast palpitations, diagnosed as AF and treated with amiodarone. His BP is now 135/72 mmHg. An ECG shows a heart rate of 78 bpm which is irregularly irregular and a right bundle branch block. There are no signs of cardiac failure. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Apixaban and electrical cardioversion in three weeks
Oral amiodarone and review in three months
Oral bisoprolol and review in three months
explanation: This patient has no past medical history of note, meaning that although he is 64 years old, attaining sinus rhythm may be possible. It is not clear how long he has been in AF for, meaning that the management of choice is anticoagulation for at least three weeks followed by cardioversion. In the event cardioversion fails, then other options could be considered,including rate control using a beta blocker with long-term anticoagulation.

stem: A 62-year-old man who had an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator(ICD) inserted nine months ago presents to the Cardiology Clinic for review. The ICD has discharged twice in the last four months and fear of the device firing has now led to him staying inside permanently and avoiding any stress and exercise. What is the most likely underlying psychiatric diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has a significant and specific phobia with respect to his ICD firing again and this is leading to a specific behaviour to avoid it,including avoidance of exercise and going out of the house. Targeted psychological therapy is the intervention of choice. In some phobias, desensitisation or exposure therapy is a potential option, but clearly exposing the patient to more firing of his defibrillator is not an option. Pharmacotherapy should be avoided if possible, given this patient's history of cardiovascular disease.

stem: A 29-year-old man is reviewed in the Oncology Clinic two months after a colectomy for colon cancer. This does not appear to be related to the development of colonic polyps,although he does appear to have a genetic cancer syndrome. What genetic abnormality is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: The MLH1 gene provides the genetic code for a protein which plays an essential role in DNA repair.The MLH1 protein forms a dimer with another protein called PMS2, which is responsible for co-ordinating DNA repair activity. It is associated with around 40% of cases of hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), also known as Lynch syndrome. Men with the condition also have an increased risk of tumours of the stomach, small intestine, gall bladder ducts,upper urinary tract and brain. Rare skin cancers, such as sebaceous adenocarcinomas, are also seen.

stem: A 75-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner complaining of severe bilateral temporal headaches. She has been taking eight paracetamol per day, with no improvement. She also tells you that she has been off her food for the past few weeks. She has hypertension, which is currently managed with ramipril and amlodipine. Her BP is 155/90 mmHg.
explanation: Giant Cell Arteritis Media explanations This patient has symptoms suggestive of temporal arteritis, but no symptoms of claudication or visual loss. It is therefore safe to commence a mid dose of prednisolone of 40 mg/day while awaiting the temporal artery biopsy. Not starting corticosteroids is potentially negligent, as the patient is at increased risk of blindness, transient ischaemic attack or stroke. An improvement in symptoms of headache is usually seen within 48 hours and once symptoms and abnormal blood tests have completely resolved, then weaning of prednisolone can begin.

stem: A35-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his wife. She is concerned as he has been fired from work for making errors and trying to complete work projects too quickly over the last few months. He seems to only sleep for two hours per night and his conversation goes off track almost all the time. He refuses to talk to you, apart from telling you his colleagues are jealous of him, he is the best performer at the office and he speaks 12 languages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has features suggestive of delusions of grandeur (including claiming to speak 12 languages) and flight of ideas, which, together with the acute lack of sleep, fit with a diagnosis of mania. The aim of treatment is to reduce symptoms rapidly and ensure the patient acts in a safe way. In the acute situation, sedation with a benzodiazepine could be considered, coupled with an atypical antipsychotic such as risperidone. Over the longer term, lithium is an option.

stem: A 27-year-old man who has coeliac disease is diagnosed with new-onset adrenal insufficiency. He wants to take once-daily corticosteroid replacement. He weighs 75 kg. What is the most appropriate daily prednisolone dose?
explanation: Guidelines recommend an adult hydrocortisone replacement dose of 15-25 mg/day in two divided doses. Prednisolone is approximately four times more potent than hydrocortisone,meaning a dose of 4 mg is correct. This may need to be doubled in patients who suffer an intercurrent illness.

stem: A 45-year-old man is referred to the Hepatology Clinic with persistent tiredness, itching and abnormal liver function tests. He is usually well and takes no regular medication. He has scratch marks over the upper body. There is two finger-breadth hepatomegaly. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 121 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 81×10/L 150-400×10/L Immunoglobulin G (lgG) 25 g/L 6.0-16.0 g/L Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 825 U/L 50 U/L Alkaline phosphatase(ALP) 141 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Bilirubin 19μmol/L 21μmol/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Autoimmune hepatitis presents with gradually worsening tiredness, reduced exercise tolerance and itching.

stem: A 49-year-old woman, who has systemic lupus erythematosus, is admitted to the Urology Ward with renal stones. She also complains of muscle weakness over the past few months. Her BP is 148/90 mmHg and her heart rate is 93 bpm and regular. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 105 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 158×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO) 16mmol/L 22-32 mmol/l Chloride (Cl-) 115 mmol/L 96-106 mmol/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Renal Tubular Acidosis explanations Distal renal tubular acidosis is associated with hypokalaemia, metabolic acidosis and renal stones. Urinary pH is above 6 and there is hypercalciuria. Autoimmune conditions, including Sjogren syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus, are recognised causes of type 1 renal tubular acidosis. Correction of hypokalaemia is the initial therapy of choice. Bicarbonate supplementation is a second-Line intervention in patients who fail to respond to potassium supplementation alone.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a flu-like illness a few days after her discharge following a caesarean section for the birth of her second child and a 3-unit blood transfusion. There is evidence of pharyngitis and cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s infection?
explanation: Given this patient's symptoms, it is likely she has been exposed to a cytomegalovirus(CMV)-positive unit of blood during her 3-unit transfusion. In immunocompetent hosts, CMV can be associated with an infectious mononucleosis-like picture, which fits with the flu-like illness and lymphadenopathy seen here. Supportive treatment only is required for infection in immunocompetent hosts. Ganciclovir and valganciclovir are typically used to treat CMV infection in immunocompromised patients.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with long-standing HIV infection presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a number of red-brown nodular lesions affecting her arms, legs and torso. They are also found within the mouth. They have increased in size and frequency over the past five months. What is the most likely cause of the lesions?
explanation: This patient's skin lesions are consistent with Kaposi's sarcoma, which occurs in patients with chronic immunosuppression.Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by human herpesvirus 8,also known as Kaposi's sarcoma- associated herpesvirus. In the first instance, measurement of HIV viral load is indicated, as is CD4 count, with intensification of HIV antiviral therapy indicated. More widespread lesions of Kaposi's sarcoma can also be managed with interferon-alpha, liposomal anthracyclines or paclitaxel.

stem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the Diabetic Nephropathy Clinic for review. Her current medications include metformin, basal bolus insulin, ramipril, amlodipine and atorvastatin. Her BP is 135/82 mmHg. Her glomerular filtration rate (GFR) has fallen to 22 ml/min from 35 ml/min six months earlier. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: At GFRs below 30 ml/min, metformin is associated with an increased risk of lactic acidosis. For this reason, guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommend stopping metformin therapy when the GFR falls below this threshold. For GFRs between 30 and 45 ml/min, dose reduction should be considered. The overall incidence of lactic acidosis is very low,estimated at six cases per 100 000 years of drug exposure.

stem: A 39-year-old man is assessed two weeks after removal of a left adrenal phaeochromocytoma. What is the most appropriate investigation to monitor this patient's post-operative prognosis?
explanation: Guidelines recommend 24-hour urinary catecholamines are measured two weeks after removal of a phaeochromocytoma. If the levels are normal, then the prognosis is excellent, although lifelong repeat testing is recommended to rule out a recurrence or metastatic disease. BP should be measured and appropriate treatment initiated if there is residual hypertension. Assuming catecholamine levels are normal, this could follow a normal guideline-directed approach.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic for control of symptoms of polycystic ovary syndrome(PCOS). Her main complaint is of having to shave her face twice per week due to beard and moustache growth. She suffered a left above-knee DVT one year ago. Her BP is 123/81mmHg and her BMI is 25 kg/m. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's hirsutism?
explanation: Eflornithine is an irreversible inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase, which promotes hair growth. When used regularly as a topical treatment for hirsutism in PCOS, it can significantly reduce the need for regular shaving. It is a pregnancy category C medication and its use in pregnancy therefore is not recommended. Where patients find it difficult to comply with regularly applying eflornithine cream, other interventions such as electrolysis may be of benefit.

stem: A 38-year-old man is referred to the Neurology Clinic. He has been suffering from multiple headaches affecting the area around his right eye. Headaches last between 15 and 90 minutes each time and they can occur up to five times each evening. He says his eye goes red and he has pain and tearing when the headache occurs. Neurological examination is entirely normal in the clinic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Short-lasting, unilateral,neuralgiform headache attacks with conjunctival injection and tearing
explanation: Unilateral headaches which occur at a similar time each evening, lasting for between 15 and 90 minutes, up to five times each evening, fit well with a diagnosis of cluster headache. Reddening of the eye and tearing are also consistent with cluster headache. The diagnosis is a clinical one. Both smoking and alcohol may precipitate attacks and patients should reduce both, if possible. Oxygen is most effective for acute attacks and verapamil can be used for prophylaxis.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic for secondary amenorrhoea. She is a gymnast and, while training for a possible place in the Olympic team, has lost 5 kg in weight over the past few months. Her BMI is 17.5 kg/m. What is the most useful investigation?
explanation: Weight loss associated with physical training is likely to have precipitated hypothalamic amenorrhoea in this patient. As such, measuring the luteinising hormone level is the most appropriate next step in investigating this patient's symptoms. In the event the level is confirmed as being low, then diet and nutrition advice to gradually increase her BMI, while maintaining her physical fitness, is advised.

stem: A 24-year-old woman, who is an IV heroin abuser, was admitted 48 hours ago to the Medical Take with night sweats, which have worsened over the last four weeks. She has a temperature of 37.8℃; her BP is 95/65 mmHg and her heart rate is 92 bpm and regular. She has an ejection systolic murmur, loudest in the aortic area. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 102 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count (WCC) 11.1×10/L 4-11×109/l Platelets (PLT) 135×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Blood cultures Gram-positive cocci in clusters What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: Infective Endocarditis explanations S. aureus is a Gram-positive coccus which forms clumps and fits with the appearance seen here on blood culture. The presence of a systolic murmur in an IV drug abuser is suggestive of infective endocarditis. Native valve S. aureus endocarditis is associated with IV drug abuse and healthcare procedures such as joint implantation. It carries a mortality of 15-20% in some case series. For methicillin-susceptible S. aureus infection, flucloxacillin, rifampicin and gentamicin are a typical regimen. Vancomycin is substituted for flucloxacillin where there is methicillin resistance.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has suffered an allergic reaction while blowing up balloons for a child's birthday party and is found to have latex allergy. To what else is she most likely to be allergic?
explanation: Bananas commonly cause a food allergy in patients with latex fruit syndrome. In total, around 50% of patients with latex allergy suffer reactions to fruits and vegetables. Common causes of food allergy include: · avocado · banana · chestnut · fig · kiwi · pepper · peach · tomato.

stem: A 20-year-old woman is referred to the Renal Clinic with persistent haematuria. This has been noted on three separate visits to the General Practitioner over the past year. She tellls you that her brother and father have the same problem, but their kidneys are working fine. Her BP is 105/72 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no masses. What is the most likely diagnosis? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 132 g/L 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 207×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine dipstick Blood 1+, protein negative
explanation: Haematuria explanations This patient has haematuria with normal renal function and normal physical examination and other family members are affected equally, raising the possibility of autosomal dominant inheritance. The most likely cause of her presentation is benign familial haematuria(BFH), with thinning of the glomerular basement membrane. In some cases of BFH, collagen gene defects have been identified.No treatment is required, unless proteinuria and renal impairment develop, in which case the diagnosis should be re-examined. Some cases of BFH may, in fact, represent autosomal recessive Alport syndrome.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with jaundice. He has been unwell with a flu-like illness over the past few days and has not been eating. He tells you he was jaundiced on one previous occasion. He has jaundiced sclerae and an abdominal examination is entirely normal. Investigation Result Normal value Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 35 U/L 50 U/L Alkaline phosphatase(ALP) 84 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Bilirubin 28μmol/L 21μmol/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Gilbert syndrome is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern and is characterised by recurrent unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, often occurring at the same time as a period of fasting ora concurrent illness, such as that seen here. It occurs because of a mutation in the gene which encodes for uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase 1A1.The isolated rise in bilirubin level is consistent with the diagnosis. Homozygous Gilbert syndrome is thought to affect between 2% and 10% of Caucasian populations.No treatment is required for Gilbert syndrome and the jaundice resolves spontaneously over a few days.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath, stridor and subcutaneous oedema. This is his third attack in the last four years and he is thought to have hereditary angio-oedema. What is most likely to be elevated at the time of an attack?
explanation: Bradykinin levels are elevated in patients who suffer from hereditary angio-oedema and are responsible for acute episodes of angio-oedema. Elevated levels cause subcutaneous and submucosal oedema; this is why urticaria is absent.C1 inhibitor levels are reduced in patients with hereditary angio-oedema, as are C4 levels during an acute episode. Recombinant C1 inhibitor is the intervention of choice. Adrenaline brings only short- term benefit.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presents to the Haematology Day Review Service with a left above-knee DVT. Her aunt and sister are carriers of the factor V Leiden mutation. Which clotting test is the best initial investigation for factor VLeiden carriage?
explanation: The dRVVT test is the initial screening test for factor V Leiden carriage. The factor V Leiden mutation stops factor V from being degraded by activated protein C.This means that patients are at increased risk of venous thrombosis. Blood samples are mixed with snake venom in the presence and absence of activated protein C.

stem: A 68-year-old man who presented to his General Practitioner with night sweats and weight loss is referred to the Haematology Clinic after an immunoglobulin G(IgG) paraprotein band measured at 32 g/L was detected. What is the optimal way to determine skeletal involvement with respect to this patient's disease?
explanation: Whole body MRI is more sensitive than a traditional plain radiograph skeletal survey with respect to detecting bony deposits from myeloma, the likely diagnosis here, making it the investigation of choice to determine skeletal involvement. Bone marrow aspirate and trephine is also required to confirm the diagnosis by determining the percentage plasma cell infiltration and immunofixation of serum and urine is usually considered to determine the paraprotein subtype. For elderly patients with a reasonable functional status who are not suitable for bone marrow transplantation, bortezomib,melphalan and prednisone are one initial option for treatment.

stem: A19-year-old man is referred to the Ophthalmology Clinic. He is finding it difficult to drive because of decreased visual acuity affecting his left eye. He also admits to muscle weakness over the past few months. Fundoscopy reveals telangiectasias and oedema affecting the left optic nerve. He has bilateral proximal muscle weakness and increased tone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is a mitochondrial disorder which is nine times more likely to affect men than women. It typically begins with progressive unilateral optic neuropathy and the other eye is usually affected months or even years afterwards. A percentage of patients also have symptoms of proximal myopathy with increased tone. Fundoscopy changes typically include telangiectasias and pseudo-oedema of the optic disc. LHON is thought to occur due to impaired glutamate transport, which increases reactive oxygen species and damage due to oxidative stress. Idebenone may be of benefit in some patients.

stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department complaining of abdominal pain and a cloudy peritoneal dialysis fluid bag which is not draining completely. His temperature is 38.5°℃. His abdomen is mildly distended and generally tender. He is clutching his last dialysis bag, which is cloudy with obvious clumps of fibrinous material. What organism is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: Coagulase-negative staphylococci, such as S.epidermidis, are the most common cause of peritonitis in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis. They are responsible for around 39% of cases overall. S. aureus is only responsible for around 4% of cases. Empirical antibiotic therapy should cover both Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms and include an agent such as vancomycin, combined with a fourth-generation cephalosporin or an aminoglycoside.

stem: A72-year-old man comes to the Neurology Clinic for review of his Parkinson's disease. He has been taking levodopa for the past three years and is now experiencing significant 'off'periods. He has failed to tolerate both ropinirole and cabergoline due to adverse effects. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Entacapone increases the levodopa area under the curve and prolongs its duration of action by blocking the activity of catechol-O-methyltransferase, the enzyme that metabolises levodopa. It can be used in combination with levodopa to reduce off-phenomena, particularly when patients do not tolerate a dopamine agonist, as is the case here. Increased dyskinesias may be seen at treatment initiation, although these usually gradually resolve. Monoamine oxidase B inhibitors, such as rasagiline, may also be used to reduce motor fluctuations.

stem: A 78-year-old man comes to the Neurology Clinic with his wife. He has suffered from memory loss, an apraxic gait and urinary incontinence over the last nine months. There is no papilloedema. What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation: There are features of normal pressure hydrocephalus here, with apraxia, incontinence and memory loss in the absence of papilloedema. The optimal way to make the diagnosis is by demonstrating an improvement to the gait and walking speed following removal of a high CSF volume by lumbar puncture. Of course, CT is essential before considering a lumbar puncture. If confirmed, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt can improve symptoms over the longer term.

stem: An 80-year-old woman who has Alzheimer's disease is admitted to the Care of the Elderly Ward with a urinary tract infection. She has severe nausea and vomiting. She usually manages in a warden-controlled flat, with supply of meals and home help. What is the most appropriate way to manage this patient's nausea and vomiting?
explanation: Ondansetron is a 5HT-3 receptor antagonist which is a centrally acting antiemetic. In this patient, there are two main considerations: to avoid excessive anticholinergic activity and to avoid dopamine antagonist antiemetics. Both cyclizine and diphenhydramine have some anticholinergic activity, meaning they should be avoided if possible. Metoclopramide and chlorpromazine are also dopamine antagonists, meaning that they should not be used here. Ondansetron can cause QT prolongation, meaning that it should be avoided in patients with long-QT syndrome.

stem: A 39-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department saying that she feels more depressed, sleepy and anxious and she is not responding to regular sertraline and psychological therapy. She tells you that she is having thoughts about taking a paracetamol overdose, as she cannot manage any more. She has been taking sertraline 200 mg once daily for over five months. She looks unkempt. Her BMI is 21kg/m. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Given this patient has failed to respond adequately to a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), one potential option is to switch medication to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor such as moclobemide. As she reports somnolence as a prominent symptom, a monoamine oxidase inhibitor is a better option than a sedating antidepressant such as amitriptyline. Tailing and switching from an SSRI to moclobemide is advised. Overall toxicity of moclobemide is less than that of other agents such as tricyclic antidepressants.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He has Marfan syndrome and asthma and has been under surveillance with annual echocardiography. His blood pressure is 135/82 mmHg and his heart rate is 78 bpm and regular. His most recent echocardiogram reveals an aortic root of 45 mm. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Trials of angiotensin receptor blockers in Marfan syndrome have suggested that they have a similar efficacy to beta blockers in protecting against aortic root dilatation. A trial comparing a higher dose of atenolol than that usually deployed suggested similar efficacy. This patient's blood pressure is above target at 135/82 mmHg, so valsartan is appropriate. Earlier trials of beta blockade targeted a heart rate of60 bpm at rest and comparative trials suggest beta blockers and angiotensin receptor blockers are potentially interchangeable. When the aortic root diameter is above 45 mm, then twice-yearly monitoring by transthoracic echocardiography is recommended. If the aortic root is growing rapidly(3mm/year), then surgery should be considered.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department having suffered a seizure while at her local pub. She has no medical illnesses and takes no regular medication, but suffered one febrile seizure as a child. According to bystanders, she had generalised twitching and was unconscious for a few minutes after the fit. She is mildly confused when you examine her in hospital. She has not bitten her tongue or been incontinent of urine. What feature is most suggestive of epilepsy?
explanation: The period of unconsciousness after this patient's seizure, coupled with residual confusion, is highly suggestive of a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Other features which could be supportive of a diagnosis of epilepsy include tongue biting and incontinence, which are absent here. A 12-lead ECG is indicated to rule out an obvious arrhythmia.MRI should be considered if epileptic seizures are felt to be focal in onset, whereas electroencephalography is useful to confirm changes in keeping with generalised-onset seizures or to determine seizure onset location if epilepsy surgery is being considered. The patient should also be told not to drive and to inform the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency.

stem: A34-year-old woman, who is an IV heroin user, presents to the Emergency Department feeling unwell. She feels her health has gone downhill over the past few months with lethargy, night sweats and anorexia. On examination,her BP is 155/90 mmHg and her heart rate is 89 bpm and regular. She has an erythematous rash, with areas of palpable purpura. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 112 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count(WCC) 6.5×10/L 4-11×10/l Platelets (PLT) 142×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 178 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Blood 2+, protein 2+ What is the most likely cause of this patient's renal impairment?
explanation: Membranous Nephropathy explanations This patient's symptoms are suggestive of cryoglobulinaemia, which, in a heroin addict, raises the possibility of hepatitis C infection. Given the degree of renal impairment, haematuria and proteinuria, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is the most likely cause of her renal impairment. It is associated with both basement membrane thickening and inflammatory cell infiltration.The condition is also seen in patients with HIV and hepatitis B infection. Type 1 membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis makes up 80- 85% of cases. Symptoms resolve with hepatitis C antiviral therapy.

stem: A32-year-old woman, who has type l diabetes and epilepsy, comes to the Diabetes Clinic because she is eight weeks pregnant. She has chronic oesophageal reflux disease and microalbuminuria. Which of the patient's medications must be discontinued immediately?
explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibitors are contraindicated in the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. Oligohydramnios, fetal and neonatal renal failure, bony malformations, limb contractures, pulmonary hypoplasia, prolonged hypotension and neonatal death are all described in conjunction with the use of ACE inhibitors after week 12 of pregnancy.Women with type I diabetes intending to become pregnant should be switched to an alternative antihypertensive medication, if possible.

stem: A73-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with flu-like symptoms and a chronic dry cough which have built steadily over the past few days. He has a severe headache and a fever. He smokes five cigarettes per day and keeps pigeons, which he races. His temperature is 38.0°℃; his BP is 110/70 mmHg and his heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. There is wheeze on auscultation of the chest. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 142 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 11.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 162×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 132 mg/l 10 mg/l Chest X-ray Extensive right lower lobe consolidation
explanation: This patient keeps pigeons and has developed a pneumonia with a subacute onset where changes on the chest ×-ray are much more significant, compared to the signs on auscultation. There is also relative bradycardia. Taken together, these features raise the possibility of infection with C.psittaci, an intracellular bacterium.Use of tetracycline or doxycycline is the usual first-Line intervention,with treatment given for 2-3 weeks to minimise the risk of relapse.

stem: A19-year-old man presents to the Cardiology Clinic with severe headaches and palpitations. His BP is 169/72 mmHg. His General Practitioner suspects he has a coarctation of the aorta. What feature on examination is most likely to localise the coarctation?
options: Differential blood pressure between the right and left arms
Muscle wasting and failure of the right arm to develop properly
explanation: The most common site of coarctation of the aorta is distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. This means that radiofemoral delay, with a reduced pulse amplitude in the lower limbs, is the most likely finding. Lower limb muscle weakness, very cold feet and neurological impairment in the lower limbs may also be seen. MRI is the optimal way to image the coarctation and determine possible operative approaches.

stem: Which two areas of the nephron are responsible for most sodium reabsorption?
options: Distal convoluted tubule and ascending loop of Henle
Distal convoluted tubule and descending loop of Henle
Proximal convoluted tubule and ascending loop of Henle
Proximal convoluted tubule and descending loop of Henle
explanation: About 60-70% of filtered sodium is reabsorbed by the proximal convoluted and straight tubules and a further 25-30% of filtered sodium is reabsorbed by the ascending loop of Henle. Although the distal convoluted tubule is responsible for a small fraction of sodium reabsorption (5-10%), this can be greatly impacted upon by agents, such as bendroflumethiazide, which act on the thiazide-sensitive sodium and chloride cotransporter in the distal tubule.

stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with severe headache, neck stiffness and decreased consciousness. According to his flatmates, he has been complaining of a sore throat over the past 48 hours. His temperature is 38.8℃;his BP is 90/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 105 bpm and regular.His GCS score is 12. He has obvious photophobia and neck stiffness, as well as a purpuric rash. What is the most appropriate next step? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 152 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 18.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 295×10/L 150-400×10/L Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) microscopy Intra-neutrophil Gram-negative diplococci
explanation: This patient's symptoms and the presence of Gram-negative diplococci on CSF examination are consistent with a diagnosis of meningococcal septicaemia. ALthough benzylpenicillin may be considered for out-of- hospital use, intravenous ceftriaxone is the intervention of choice. An intravenous dose of 2g,repeated every 12 hours, is recommended. Guidelines support a 5-day course initially. Where an inadequate response is seen by five days, treatment is extended to seven days. Bacterial Meningitis Media explanations.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with small joint polyarthritis affecting his hands, which is making it difficult for him to work as a computer programmer. He also has pain in his wrists and feet. Examination reveals distal interphalangeal joint arthritis; there is also nail pitting. There is a small patch of erythematous scaling skin next to his umbilicus. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: This patient has nail pitting and a small patch of psoriasis next to the umbilicus. Although the pattern of joint involvement follows a rheumatoid-type pattern, the most likely diagnosis is likely to be psoriatic arthritis.An asymmetrical pauciarticular pattern of presentation is also seen. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C- reactive protein levels are usually elevated, although rheumatoid factor is usually negative. A positive rheumatoid factor does not rule out psoriatic arthritis, as 10-15% of the population are rheumatoid factor- positive. Like rheumatoid arthritis, methotrexate is an initial disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug of choice. Q. Psoriatic Arthritis Answered Flagged Media explanations.

stem: A 28-year-old man who has osteosarcoma of the left femur with lung metastases presents to the Emergency Department with severe bony ache, which has not been relieved by regular paracetamol. He has said that the pain is so bad that he just wants to die. His BP is 155/88 mmHg and his heart rate is 99 bpm and regular. His body mass index is 21 kg/m. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 184×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 115μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l What is the most appropriate way to manage this patient's analgesia?
explanation: Although the next obvious step up in the analgesic ladder would be a NSAID such as naproxen, this patient is agitated and in severe pain. As such, there is an urgent need to establish effective analgesia.The best way to do this is with morphine sulfate, which can be administered orally at a dose of 15-30 mg every four hours. Once pain control is established, the total daily dose can be converted to a twice-daily dose of slow-release morphine. Pain relief - palliative care explanations.

stem: A 47-year-old man is referred to the Cardiology Clinic complaining of shortness of breath on exercise. He has impaired fasting glucose and takes amlodipine for treatment of hypertension. His BP is 145/85 mmHg and his heart rate is 84 bpm and regular. His chest is clear on auscultation. His BMI is 36 kg/m. Investigation Result Normal value Pulmonary artery pressure 26 mmHg 8-20 mmHg Ejection fraction N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) 1250 pg/ml 400 pg/ml Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 95 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Chronic thromboembolic disease with pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Pulmonary hypertension and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
explanation: This obese patient has symptoms of heart failure, coupled with an elevated NT-proBNP level, preserved ejection fraction and raised pulmonary artery pressure. This is consistent with a diagnosis of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and pulmonary hypertension. It is known as pulmonary hypertension type 2 under the World Health Organization (WHO) classification. Given the BMI is 36 kg/m,weight loss is the most important intervention. A weight loss of 10% or more will significantly improve his heart failure symptoms and likely lead to a reduction in pulmonary artery pressure. Cardiac Failure Media explanations.
